title: Agents Inside The Board
eyebrow: Your four pains: two fixed, two building — and the whole app is now one shell.

questions.ask: The other brand of agent, Codex, is not installed on this machine and cannot be signed in by me. Do you want it now?

options.label: Install it and sign in — I will build the Codex half next
Leave it. Finish everything else and Codex becomes its own job later

content.label: The four things you found on your copy
content.lead: Three of them are one cause: the app was identifying a conversation by its file on disk instead of asking Claude what it is. The fourth is Claude refusing to be in two places at once, which it is right to do.

rows: Every chat called "Started in a terminal"
The list was built by reading file names off the disk — a name and a timestamp, nothing else.
Each row is the conversation's own name, the one Claude holds for it.
No card, no folder on a row
Same cause: nothing but a file name was known about a chat the app had not run itself.

A second line per row: a chip for each card the chat worked on, which opens that card, and a chip naming the folder it ran in — so two chats on the same project in different trees are told apart at a glance.
A "Resume all" button
Mine, from the first sketch of the restore list.
Gone, and the rule behind it with it. Forty agents starting at once is a bill nobody meant to sign.
"Currently running as a background agent" when you opened a chat
You opened the conversation that is answering you right now. Claude refuses to attach to a live session twice, and that refusal is correct — two windows writing one transcript would corrupt it.
Building: the row will say it is running elsewhere before you click, open for reading, and offer to carry on in a copy.
Nothing said before — a resumed chat opened blank
The window replays the app's own record of a chat, and there is no record of a conversation the app never ran.
Building: Claude hands over the earlier turns and the window reads them in — which also fills in the card chips for chats begun in a terminal.

blocks.label: Watch it happen: 127.0.0.1:3007
blocks.text: A second address now serves the app straight from the merged code, so anything I land shows up on a refresh — no rebuild, no reinstall, no waiting for me. Your usual address keeps working exactly as before; use this one while I am building. It reads the same board and the same chats, so nothing about it is a copy.

blocks.label: The rule that changed
blocks.text: The app used to refuse to look inside a conversation at all, because the file format is documented as unstable. It no longer has to guess: Claude publishes what its sessions are called, where they ran, and what was said in them. We ask; we still never parse a file ourselves.

blocks.label: Watch it happen: 127.0.0.1:3007
blocks.text: That address serves the merged code straight from the checkout and reads your real board, so anything landed shows on a refresh — no rebuild, no restart, nothing to wait for. Your usual 127.0.0.1:3008 has been rebuilt with all of this too.

blocks.label: The list of 319 chats was measured before anything was built for it
blocks.text: First row on screen 1.7 seconds after the address, all 319 there twelve milliseconds later, and dragging the list end to end costs sixteen milliseconds a step. Nothing to fix, so nothing was built — a list that draws in one go and scrolls at full speed has nothing to gain from being cut into pieces, and cutting it would cost the sticky day headings and the browser's own find-on-page.

content.label: Your four pains, and what fixes each
content.lead: Each one is a separate mechanism, and each is confirmed to work — not assumed.

rows: No way to see which card a chat worked on
The app watches every move the agent makes and writes the link itself — chat to card, card to chat, report to both. Nobody has to remember anything.
A report forces a trip to another tab
The report appears inside the chat; a click opens it large in place — same page, still never leaving this machine.
Every restart means bringing windows back one by one
The app lists yesterday's conversations under each project, each under its own name. One click brings one back.
Pictures do not show in the terminal
Any picture the agent makes or names appears in the conversation as a picture.

before.caption: Before: a project list and a board — nowhere to talk, nothing linked

after.caption: Now: a conversation in the app — the answer streamed in, the tool feed underneath, and the agent stopped on a permission ask with three buttons

content.label: The first pieces, live
content.lead: Built and proved on screen: the conversation streams and stops on a clickable permission ask, and one turn later the whole transcript vocabulary is there.

shots.caption: After the click: the ask collapsed to Allowed, the tool row turned green, the file was written, and the turn's cost — five and a half cents — sits in the corner

One finished turn showing the full vocabulary: every tool as a row, a helper's work nested under the call that made it, the changed lines side by side, your picture in the message — the answer names its colours, so it truly reached the agent — the running checklist, and the spend

blocks.label: Your screen rule earned its keep twice in two days
blocks.text: First: every signal behind the screen said working while the window showed an empty bubble — streamed words filed under the wrong name. Then: the header claimed a permission setting the session was not actually in — fixed text no test would ever catch. Both found only by looking at the picture, which is exactly the rule you set.
One thing waits on you, with no hurry: when the build reaches the Codex piece, that tool has to be installed on this machine and signed in once with your account. Nothing before it waits.

content.label: The joins, live
content.lead: The links you asked for are working: chat to card, card to chat, report to both — recorded by the app watching the work, read back from the board itself.

shots.caption: The card's own panel: its pieces ticked as they close, its timeline, and the chat that touched it listed at the bottom — click it and you land back in that exact conversation
A report the chat made, opened large over the dimmed conversation — its checklist is read live from the card's pieces, and it closes with its own button

content.label: Yesterday's conversations, back after a restart
content.lead: Close the app, reopen it, and every chat is still there — including ones you started in a terminal, each under its own name.

shots.caption: Your own machine, live: 319 conversations under this project, each one under the name Claude gave it, grouped by the day, with the folder it ran in beneath — where every row used to read "Started in a terminal"
One click on a conversation begun in a terminal, and it answers again in the app — same conversation, not a new one

blocks.label: It was offering and not coming back
blocks.text: A chat the app already knew stayed grey however many times you pressed the button, because coming back was never recorded anywhere. It is now, and a resume that fails says so instead of looking slow.

content.label: It follows you around, and it remembers
content.lead: Four more pieces are on your copy: what is waiting on you wherever you are, a card that says it is being worked on, a chat you start from a card, and one search across everything ever said.

shots.caption: Seen from the project list, which belongs to neither project: two chats stopped for your say-so, each naming its project and what it is asking about — click one and you land on it with the question on screen
A card being worked on says so on the board, with a live line of what the chat is doing this second — and a Start chat button that opens a conversation already briefed on that card
One word said in two chats in two projects, found from anywhere: the sentence it fell in, the word marked, and the project named
What it cost, per day, per project — two charts and never one, because one brand bills money and the other counts tokens
The same conversation on a phone: the list of chats becomes a drawer, the composer stays in reach

blocks.label: A day of it was one trap
blocks.text: A test run started the app without first taking its ports, so a leftover from an earlier run kept answering — the browser was served yesterday's build while every log said the run was fresh. It now takes its ports first and stops if it cannot.

blocks.label: How it stays brand-neutral
blocks.text: Each brand is driven in its own official channel, behind one thin shared shape of ours — so a third brand is one new driver, not a rebuild. An open shared standard for this exists (several code editors use it), but for your two brands it has confirmed holes today exactly where you care: cost arrives empty for Codex through it, and picking up a terminal session through it is unproven. It stays on the shelf until a third brand matters.

blocks.label: Two honest differences
blocks.text: Only Claude asks you multiple-choice clarifying questions mid-work; Codex never does. And the typed-command menu you kept is confirmed working on Claude but unproven on Codex — that is being settled against sources before it is built. Where a brand lacks an ability, its window simply does not show that button; it never imitates one.

content.label: The six additions, all in
content.lead: Your answer: take all six from the start.

items: A waiting-on-you tray: one list, across every project, of chats stopped and waiting for you — a permission ask, a question, finished work — with a count on it.
Start a chat from a card: click a card, the conversation opens already briefed on it, and the link between them exists from birth.
A glance strip: every running chat's current line on one screen, like seeing all your terminals at once.
Answer from your phone: the same pages reachable from the sofa, on your home network only.
Search across every conversation ever had.
A spend line per project and per day.

decisions.title: Each brand of agent is driven in its own official channel, behind one thin shared shape of ours
decisions.why: Revised now that the tool must work with any brand. For your two brands, everything you asked for is confirmed on the direct path today; the open shared standard has confirmed holes exactly there and adds a third-party part that has already been archived and renamed once. A third brand later is one new driver — or the shared standard, by then matured.

decisions.title: A small helper runs beside the board rather than rebuilding the board's engine
decisions.why: Fastest route, and it leaves the board's own program untouched so upstream updates still merge cleanly. It can be folded in later without changing what you see.

decisions.title: A conversation and its cards are joined from both sides, not nested one inside the other
decisions.why: Revised to match your goal: chats live in their own tab with a sidebar, cards in theirs, and each shows the other — a chat lists the cards it touched, a card lists the chats that touched it, reports link to both.

decisions.title: We stop at the features you named and do not chase the terminal
decisions.why: The terminal gains new behaviour every few weeks. Chasing it turns a one-month build into permanent maintenance.

decisions.title: It signs in with your subscription, never with a pay-as-you-go key
decisions.why: This is the only decision that could turn a free conversation into a metered one, so it is written down rather than left to whoever sets it up. The same rule holds for every brand: the app reuses the sign-in you already did in the terminal.

decisions.title: No outside tool services are plugged in unless you ask for one
decisions.why: Each one attaches its full instruction sheet to every message for the life of the session, used or not. That is the real cost you had heard about, and the way to not pay it is to not add them.

decisions.title: The link between a chat and a card is written by the machine, never remembered by the agent
decisions.why: The app sees every tool the agent uses as it happens, so the link is recorded at the moment of touch. Asking the agent to remember is how links go missing.

decisions.title: After a restart, yesterday's conversations come back as a list, one click each — and there is no button that starts all of them
decisions.why: An agent that wakes itself and starts working unattended is a bill and a surprise. Revised on your word: the same objection applies to one button that wakes forty of them, so it is gone.

decisions.title: Reports stay on this machine; the chat shows the same page inline and large on click
decisions.why: The report pages already exist and already refuse the cloud. The viewer is new; the report path and its refusal are untouched.

decisions.title: Two tabs per project, chat and board, as you said — reports get no third tab
decisions.why: Reports appear inside the chats they came from and in the side lists. A third tab would be a second home for the same pages.

decisions.title: A card being worked on shows its chat on the board, live
decisions.why: The board tile and the conversation are two views of the same work, so claiming a card and being its chat are the same fact.

decisions.title: Cost is shown as the agent itself reports it, never computed by us
decisions.why: Claude reports dollars; Codex reports only a usage count. A price table of our own would rot and quietly lie; showing what the brand reports never does.

decisions.title: Where a brand lacks an ability, the window hides that button rather than imitating it
decisions.why: A faked button is a promise the agent underneath cannot keep. The window stays honest about what each brand can do.

decisions.title: The chat ships the keep set plus the typed-command menu; everything else on the menu is out
decisions.why: Your answer: the typed commands are very important, the rest is fine to drop. The menu above records the final state of every row.

decisions.title: Agents run on this computer only; reaching other machines is its own later job, on the board
decisions.why: Your answer: start here, reaching other machines can come later. It is a card now, so it cannot be forgotten or quietly grow into this build.

decisions.title: All six additions are in from the start
decisions.why: Your answer, verbatim: take all six additions from the start.

decisions.title: Every piece of this job is judged by looking at the screen it produces, and behaviour is proved by driving the app like a user
decisions.why: Your standing rule for this work: check the screen output to make sure it works nice, and exercise behaviour through the browser's own developer tools rather than reasoning about code. The browser-driving service is wired into the repo so every session can obey this.

decisions.title: A card is linked when the chat acted on it, never when something merely mentioned it
decisions.why: A board command naming the card, or a file written under its name, counts. A mention in the agent's prose, in tool output, or in your own message does not — reading a document that cites a card is not working on it. A wrong chip is worse than a missing one.

decisions.title: A conversation keeps its place in the list when it comes back
decisions.body: A chat begun in a terminal becomes one of the app's own the moment you resume it. It stays the row you pressed rather than jumping somewhere else in the list, because it is the same conversation.
decisions.why: A row that changes identity the moment you act on it reads as two different chats, and you would not know which one you had just woken.

decisions.title: A card is linked to a chat the moment you start one from it
decisions.why: Pressing Start chat on a card is you saying the two belong together. Waiting to infer it from what the agent does would leave the board blank for the first minute of every conversation.

decisions.title: A chat is identified by what Claude calls it, its cards and its folder — never by a file on disk
decisions.why: Your words: the row should read as a name, then the card and the tree. A file name is not an identity, which is why every row said the same thing. Claude publishes all three, so the app asks rather than guesses.

decisions.title: Opening a chat is reading it; only typing in it starts an agent
decisions.why: Reading what was already said costs nothing and starts nothing, so it must never fail — including for a conversation running somewhere else this second. That one opens for reading and offers to carry on in a copy, because two windows writing one transcript would ruin it.

decisions.title: The whole app is one shell: two bars that never move, and only the work underneath scrolls
decisions.why: Your instruction. Four bars stacked before any work showed, and all of them slid away as you read. From here every screen is built from one set of parts — one place defines a chip, a button, a panel — so the app reads as one product instead of five.

decisions.title: A tab carries its own tools into the second bar
decisions.why: The board's filter row alone is eleven controls with their own state; the bar borrows them where they stand rather than the page above collecting them, so adding a tool to a tab never touches the shell.

decisions.title: The long list is left whole, because it was measured first
decisions.why: 319 chats draw in one paint and scroll at frame rate, so the machinery for cutting a list into pieces would buy nothing and cost the sticky headings and find-on-page. If the numbers ever turn, that is when it earns it.

next.if_nothing: Everything above is live on 127.0.0.1:3007 and on your usual 127.0.0.1:3008. The build carries on down this list, one merge at a time so you can test each on its own.
